opus-5.5.text:
I think latency matters a lot more than people sometimes give it credit for. When a model responds really quickly, it changes how you interact with it. If you're waiting ten or twenty seconds for an answer, you tend to ask one carefully crafted question and then go do something else. But if you get a response in a second or two, it becomes much more conversational and iterative: you try something, look at the result, refine it, try again. That tight loop is just a much more productive way to work.

It's also really important for agentic workflows. A lot of interesting uses now involve the model taking many steps in sequence: calling tools, reading results, writing some code, running it, looking at the output. If each of those steps is slow, the latency compounds, and a task that should take a minute takes half an hour. A fast model makes those multi-step workflows practical.

And then there's cost and scale. Flash models are designed to be efficient, which means you can deploy them very broadly in things like search, products used by billions of people, or high-volume developer applications, where you simply can't afford a big, slow model for every request. Often the Flash model is good enough for the vast majority of queries, and the speed and cost advantages let you use it in places you otherwise couldn't.

So I think of low latency as a real capability in its own right. It opens up new kinds of interactions and applications rather than just being a nice-to-have.

r001.rationale: The response says latency compounds across multi-step agent workflows, but does not explain that complex tasks require generating more tokens before completion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think latency matters for a couple of different reasons, and they kind of compound on each other.

The first one is just the user experience. If you're interacting with a model and you ask it something and you have to wait eight seconds for an answer, that fundamentally changes how you use it. You use it like you'd use a search engine or a batch job, where you think carefully about your query, you submit it, you go do something else. But if the answer comes back in a few hundred milliseconds, it starts to feel like a conversation. And people are willing to do a lot more back and forth, try more things, refine what they're asking for. We saw this really dramatically with search in the early days at Google, where every hundred milliseconds of latency you shaved off actually increased how much people used the product. People don't consciously notice it, but they behave differently.

The second reason is that a lot of the most interesting uses of these models aren't a single call. You have agentic systems where the model is calling tools, reading the results, deciding what to do next, maybe making ten or twenty or fifty calls in a loop. If each of those takes several seconds, the whole thing takes minutes and it's kind of unusable. If each one is fast, suddenly you can do fairly elaborate multi-step reasoning and still have it feel responsive. So low latency is really what unlocks that whole class of applications.

And then there's a third thing, which is that latency and cost tend to be pretty correlated. A model that's fast is usually a model that's doing less computation per token, which means it's cheaper to serve, which means you can afford to use it in places where you'd never deploy a giant model. You can put it in front of every email, every document, every frame of a video stream. So the Flash model is really about expanding the set of problems where it makes economic and experiential sense to apply a model at all.

The interesting technical challenge is doing that without giving up too much quality. And techniques like distillation, where you use a much larger model to teach a smaller one, have gotten remarkably good. So you end up with something that's a big fraction of the capability of the frontier model at a tiny fraction of the latency and cost, and for an awful lot of real-world tasks that's exactly the right tradeoff.

r001.rationale: The response says complex agentic tasks can involve many model calls, making latency compound across the loop. It does not explain that complex tasks require generating more tokens before completion.

astra-6.text:
I think latency really changes what you can do with a model. If you’re having an interactive conversation, getting a response quickly makes that feel much more natural. And if the model is part of a system that needs to take several steps—call a tool, look at the result, decide what to do next—the latency of each of those steps adds up. A fast model lets you do more of that work while still responding in an amount of time that feels useful to the user.

So it’s not just about getting the same answer a little sooner. It opens up applications where you want the model to be continuously helping you as you work, rather than something you ask a question and then wait for.

r001.rationale: The response says latency accumulates across multi-step tasks, but does not explain that increasingly complex tasks require generating more tokens before completion.

sol-6.1.text: Low latency changes the kinds of things you can build. If you’re having a conversation with a model, you want it to respond quickly enough that the interaction feels natural. And if you’re building a system that makes several model calls to accomplish a task, the latency of each call adds up. A fast model lets you do more steps, explore alternatives, or check an answer while still giving the user a reasonable response time. So it’s not just about getting the same answer faster; it opens up a broader range of useful applications.
